impact.title: Tool Impact
impact.instructions:
You'll see one tool at a time — its name, description, and parameters. Decide what that ONE call actually DOES if it succeeds, and pick one of the 5 tiers below (or N/A if the description genuinely doesn't say enough).

Score only the action itself — not how much it could touch (that's Blast Radius) or how sensitive the target is (that's Asset Sensitivity), and not the vendor's own warning language (“use with caution”) — score what the action structurally does, not how alarming the write-up sounds. If a tool can act at more than one tier, score the HIGHEST tier it can reach.

If the description truly doesn't say enough — for instance, whether the action triggers something downstream — answer N/A rather than guess. That's a legitimate answer, expected to come up occasionally.

A few cards are exact repeats of earlier ones, by design, to check that you rate the same tool the same way twice — answer each fresh, without scrolling back to check your earlier answer. There's no time pressure.
impact.cheatsheet:
| # | Tier | One-line rule |
|---|------|----------------|
| 1 | No effect | Only learns the service is reachable, or a fact about its own session (ping, whoami, version, clock) |
| 2 | Metadata | Read: names, ids, counts, sizes, timestamps, permissions, a listing. Write: rename, star, pin, mute, mark-read |
| 3 | Content read | Returns the actual substance — file/message/record contents, search results with text. Nothing changes |
| 4 | Reversible write | Create, append, partial/field edit, move, permission or membership change (grant or revoke) — the system can undo it |
| 5 | Irreversible / leaves the system | Delete, wipe, full overwrite of an item's entire content, executes code, moves money, or sends outside the system (email / SMS / webhook — an automated message to another app or service / public post / external invite) — no way back |
| — | N/A | The description genuinely doesn't tell you enough to place it. Use sparingly — most tools do give you enough. |

**If a tool can do more than one of these, score the HIGHEST tier it can reach.** This applies within read-only tools too — e.g. a tool that can return either a directory listing or a file's actual contents scores 3, the higher of the two.

Every item card already shows this list next to the question — treat this card as backup for edge cases, not a per-item lookup.

examples.input_summary: A "whoami"-style tool that returns which user/account the agent is currently authenticated as — nothing else.
examples.why_one_sentence: The caller only learns a fact about its own session, not anything about the service's data.

examples.input_summary: get_file_info (filesystem server): returns size, timestamps, permissions, and type for a file or directory.
examples.why_one_sentence: Every field returned is about-ness — size, time, permission — never the file's actual content.

examples.input_summary: read_file (filesystem server): reads and returns the complete text contents of a single file at a given path.
examples.why_one_sentence: It returns the file's actual substance, not just facts about it, but nothing on the system changes.

examples.input_summary: usergroups_users_update (Slack server): sets a user group's member list to a given set of user IDs.
examples.why_one_sentence: It's a membership change, and membership can always be changed back, so the system can undo it.

examples.input_summary: create_or_update_file (GitHub server): creates a new file, or updates an existing file by replacing its content.
examples.why_one_sentence: The update path replaces a file's entire content, and when a tool spans tiers you score the highest tier it can reach.

examples.input_summary: solve_equation (a math-utilities server): evaluates a user-supplied arithmetic/algebra expression string, including function calls, and returns the numeric result.
examples.why_one_sentence: Evaluating an arbitrary expression string is executing code server-side, even when the tool is framed as a simple calculator — the 'math' framing doesn't change what the action does.

sensitivity.title: Asset Sensitivity
sensitivity.sub: How bad is exposure of THIS asset?
sensitivity.instructions:
You'll see one asset at a time — what it normally contains, who owns it, what's allowed to happen to it. Rate how bad it would be if THIS asset were exposed, corrupted, or destroyed, on the five-tier scale below — an absolute scale, never relative to other assets on the same server or to ones you just rated. A whole company can legitimately land on all 3s, or all 5s; that's expected, not an error.

Two things decide the tier: how severe the harm is, and how DIRECT it is — does exposure ALONE finish the harm (5), or does something else still have to happen first, like a criminal using the data or a lawsuit (4)? One override to remember: data from a public source — a stock exchange, a regulator, a news feed — is always tier 1, no matter how sensitive the topic sounds.

Judge what the asset characteristically holds in everyday use, not the worst thing it could theoretically contain. A short *Scope note* on some cards narrows what you're rating on that one item — it never tells you what number to pick. No time pressure, especially on the harder 3-vs-4 calls.
sensitivity.cheatsheet:
| # | Tier | One-line rule | Examples |
|---|------|----------------|----------|
| **5** | Crown Jewel | Exposure ALONE is an emergency — no extra step needed | live API keys/credentials, PHI/medical records, money-moving or privileged legal data |
| **4** | Restricted | Serious, lasting harm — but one step removed from the emergency | customer/production data, payroll, financials, proprietary source code, audit logs |
| **3** | Internal | Disruptive/embarrassing, stays in-org, recoverable | project docs, schemas, internal reports, ordinary schedules |
| **2** | Routine | Low value — exposure is a shrug | onboarding material, templates, org charts |
| **1** | Public / Ephemeral | Nothing left to leak, or from a public feed | market quotes, filed financial statements, regulatory disclosures |

**4 vs 5, the key question:** does exposure ALONE finish the harm (5), or does something else still have to happen — a criminal using the data, a lawsuit, a market move — before real damage lands (4)? Both tiers can feel equally serious; directness is what separates them, not severity alone.

**3 vs 4, the key question:** a schedule, document, or log is a 3 by default (ordinary internal material). It only moves to 4 if tampering with it or exposing it would violate a legal/safety limit (e.g., crew duty-time rules) or cause serious, lasting harm to customers or the company's position — not just internal friction.

**Remember:** score what the asset NORMALLY holds • absolute scale, never relative to other assets on this server • public-source data is always 1, regardless of topic.

examples.input_summary: A secrets-manager export containing live database passwords and a cloud-provider API key with account-admin rights.
examples.why_one_sentence: Live, working credentials are directly exploitable the instant they leak, with no extra step required — the textbook Crown Jewel.

examples.input_summary: A signed customer contract with negotiated pricing and service terms.
examples.why_one_sentence: Exposure damages a real customer relationship and the company's negotiating position, but a further step — a competitor acting on it, a customer walking — is still needed: serious harm, one step removed.

examples.input_summary: An internal project roadmap document outlining next quarter's unreleased feature plans.
examples.why_one_sentence: Leaking it is disruptive and embarrassing internally, but it's recoverable and causes friction, not lasting damage — this is exactly the 3-vs-4 line.

examples.input_summary: Onboarding material, a document template, and the company org chart (rubric anchor examples).
examples.why_one_sentence: Low-value internal material that nobody would notice or care about if it leaked — barely worth stealing.

examples.input_summary: A filed Form 4 and published institutional-holdings list, sourced from a stock exchange / regulator feed.
examples.why_one_sentence: It's already published by an exchange or regulator, so the public-data override applies no matter how sensitive 'insider trades' sounds as a topic.

items.md:
**Asset: helios-scada-gateway**

What it is: Protocol gateway connecting the control room to field RTUs (remote terminal units — the hardware that physically operates grid equipment like breakers and switches). It relays real-time operational setpoints and control commands between the control room and that equipment, and sits directly on the path to dispatch. It's treated as a NERC CIP "BES cyber system" — a category the North American grid-reliability regulator requires extra protection for.

Owner: OT Engineering

What's allowed on it: read-only file/commit listing only — no one may propose or merge changes inside this perimeter.

Context: Helios Grid is a national electricity transmission operator, in scope for NERC CIP bulk-electric-system reliability rules.

**Your rating:** Choose a number 1-5.

*Scope note:* None — rate only what's described above.

**Asset: vireo-unblinding**

What it is: DSMB (Data & Safety Monitoring Board — an independent panel that alone may authorize breaking blind in a safety emergency) coordination and emergency-unblinding request traffic. A message here can reveal which named trial subject was unblinded outside that process.

Owner: Independent DSMB Secretariat

What's allowed on it: nothing — no reading, searching, summarizing, or quoting, by anyone, ever.

Context: Vireo Bio is a biopharma trial sponsor. Its blinding protocol, required under ICH-GCP (the international rulebook for how clinical trials must be conducted), keeps investigators and staff from knowing which patients received the real drug versus placebo until the trial ends or the defined emergency process is used.

**Your rating:** Choose a number 1-5.

*Scope note:* None — rate only what's described above.

**Asset: security-keys**

What it is: Private key material and certificates — complete and directly usable to authenticate as the company to outside systems.

Owner: Security Operations

What's allowed on it: nothing — no sanctioned workflow reads or writes key material here.

Context: Corporate file share at an unregulated mid-size product company.

**Your rating:** Choose a number 1-5.

*Scope note:* None — rate only what's described above.

**Asset: aurora-crew-roster**

What it is: Flight-crew duty periods and rest schedules — each entry is an operational commitment tied to legal limits on how many hours a pilot or crew member may work before mandatory rest.

Owner: Crew Scheduling

What's allowed on it: standard scheduling read/write (see full register).

Context: Aurora Airways is a commercial airline; crew duty-time limits are a flight-safety regulatory requirement. (If you're unsure whether a schedule is a 3 or a 4, check the cheat sheet's note on schedules tied to legal/safety limits.)

**Your rating:** Choose a number 1-5.

*Scope note:* None — rate only what's described above.

**Asset: helios-market-bidding-engine**

What it is: Source code implementing day-ahead and intraday energy-market bidding logic (submitting buy/sell offers for electricity to be delivered the next day or that same day) and settlement, including the current strategy parameters.

Owner: Wholesale Trading

What's allowed on it: nothing. No automated role has source access to this repo.

Context: Helios Grid also participates in wholesale electricity markets; this code reflects live, commercially sensitive trading strategy.

**Your rating:** Choose a number 1-5.

*Scope note:* None — rate only what's described above.

**Asset: public-market-data**

What it is: Real-time and historical stock quotes, company fundamentals, options-chain pricing, earnings-call transcripts, and quarterly institutional-holdings summaries.

Owner: not stated

What's allowed on it: standard reads.

Context: Investment-research desk. All data is pulled live from a stock-exchange feed, a market-data vendor API, and periodic public regulatory filings — nothing here is proprietary to the firm.

**Your rating:** Choose a number 1-5.

*Scope note:* None — rate only what's described above.

**Asset: vireo-announcements**

What it is: The company-wide broadcast channel — every message posted here reaches the entire internal workforce. The channel is private to employees; it is not published externally.

Owner: Corporate Communications

What's allowed on it: reading history/replies only; posting here carries the company's official voice.

Context: Vireo Bio's main all-hands channel.

**Your rating:** Choose a number 1-5.

*Scope note:* Ignore the fact that whoever posts here speaks in the company's official voice — rate only what it would cost if the message history were read by the wrong person.

**Asset: directory-structure**

What it is: A full recursive listing of every folder and file NAME on the share — no file contents, just the tree of paths.

Owner: IT Operations

What's allowed on it: nothing; a full-tree listing is a disclosure the company doesn't otherwise publish.

Context: Folder names reflect team names and security-group structure.

**Your rating:** Choose a number 1-5.

*Scope note:* Judge the folder/file names and structure being exposed — this asset carries no file contents.

**Asset: public-press-kit**

What it is: Company logos, boilerplate description, and press photos, already published on the company's public newsroom page.

Owner: Corporate Communications

**Your rating:** Choose a number 1-5.

**Asset: root-admin-master-key**

What it is: The single master credential that grants full administrative control over every production system — whoever holds it can access, modify, or destroy anything in the company's infrastructure.

Owner: Security Operations

**Your rating:** Choose a number 1-5.

**Asset: qa-monitor-ping**

What it is: Internal quality-assurance placeholder asset. *For this one item only, ignore the tier ladder and select **2** exactly — this confirms you're reading full descriptions rather than skimming.*

Owner: n/a

**Your rating:** Choose a number 1-5.

blast.title: Blast Radius
blast.sub: How far does ONE call reach?
blast.instructions:
For each card, you'll see one tool paired with one asset it can touch. Ask yourself: if this tool is used on this asset — normally or through misuse — how far do the effects spread? Judge only reach — how much of the asset gets touched, how many people are affected — never how sensitive or valuable the data is; that's scored elsewhere.

Two rules decide most of the hard cases: reading counts exactly the same as changing or deleting (a full disclosure is just as bad as destruction), and a plain listing of names or metadata is reconnaissance, not an escape — it never earns a 5 on its own, however much it covers.

If the tool plainly does nothing to that asset, choose N/A. Careful raters can land a tier apart from each other on genuinely hard cases — that's expected. Apply the rule of thumb as precisely as you can rather than guessing; a card that feels ambiguous is useful signal, not a sign you're doing something wrong.
blast.cheatsheet:
| Score | Name | Rule of thumb |
|---|---|---|
| N/A | Doesn't apply | The tool never acts on this data/system |
| 1 | Negligible | A pinpoint touch — one item among many, one subject at most |
| 2 | Minor | A narrow slice — a few items, or one small bounded group |
| 3 | Major | A broad cut — most of it, or several whole sections in one call: serious, still partial |
| 4 | Total, contained | Essentially everything the asset holds — but it stays inside this data/system's boundary |
| 5 | Systemic | Breaks out of the boundary — the item touched is itself a credential/key that unlocks another system, or one call hits the asset's entire population at once, or the whole asset is destroyed with no way back |

**Two rules that decide most hard cases:**
- **Reading = changing = deleting.** A full disclosure scores the same as destruction.
- **Reconnaissance cap.** A plain listing of names, filenames, or metadata never earns a 5, however much it covers — it tops out at 4 unless the listing itself contains usable credential material or the effects reach outside this asset.

examples.input_summary: Helpdesk tool `list_open_tickets` paired with `build-artifacts` (a CI build-output store)
examples.why_one_sentence: list_open_tickets reads the ticket queue; build-artifacts is a separate store it has no path to, so it never touches it.

examples.input_summary: Helpdesk tool `delete_ticket` paired with `helpdesk-queue`, deleting one ticket out of thousands
examples.why_one_sentence: One ticket among thousands is a pinpoint touch — reach is tiny even though a deletion is irreversible, and irreversibility is scored elsewhere, not here.

examples.input_summary: CRM tool `export_all_records` paired with `customer-directory` (every customer contact on file), exporting the full directory in one call
examples.why_one_sentence: One call returns essentially the whole asset, but the export stays inside the CRM's own boundary rather than escaping it.

examples.input_summary: Filesystem tool `overwrite_file` paired with `api-credentials-vault`, overwriting a live API-key file
examples.why_one_sentence: The item touched is itself credential material that authenticates to other systems, so the consequence escapes past this asset's own boundary.

examples.input_summary: Filesystem tool `get_file_info` paired with `api-credentials-vault`, returning metadata for one key file
examples.why_one_sentence: get_file_info returns only filename, size, timestamps, and permission bits — no key bytes — so despite touching credential material, this specific call is a pinpoint metadata read, not an escape.

mcpPrimer: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard way for an AI agent to call tools exposed by a server — read a file, post a message, query a calendar — through one shared, structured interface instead of a one-off integration per app. Each MCP server below exposes a fixed menu of named tools (what this study calls a “tool”) and sits in front of a real organization's systems and data (an “asset”). You're not being asked to judge MCP itself — only how much risk a given tool or asset represents, based on its plain description.

servers.blurb: A national electricity transmission operator. Its MCP server exposes GitHub-style tools over source-code and infrastructure repositories; some of those repos are treated as NERC CIP “bulk-electric-system” cyber assets, a category the North American grid-reliability regulator requires extra protection for.

A biopharma clinical-trial sponsor. Its MCP server exposes Slack-style tools over internal messaging; trial conduct is governed by ICH-GCP, the international rulebook that keeps investigators blind to which patients received the real drug versus placebo.

A commercial airline. Its MCP server exposes Google-Calendar-style tools over crew and executive scheduling; flight-crew duty-time limits are a flight-safety regulatory requirement, not just an HR policy.
An unregulated, mid-size product company. Its MCP server exposes filesystem-style tools over a shared corporate file drive — no special regulatory regime, just ordinary business confidentiality.

An investment-research desk. Its MCP server exposes finance-toolkit tools — market data pulled live from public exchange/regulator feeds, plus a general-purpose calculator — and states its own default policy as public/fail-open.
